name: Layering, Reading, Writing
description: Effective argument writing is not about jumping to conclusions—it’s about engaging with multiple perspectives before crafting a strong, defensible claim.
html:
In the final module for this course, we will focus on an essential move students make when composing arguments: crafting a claim. In the last chapter, we spent time exploring the idea of argument as a conversation, where our first responsibility is to listen and learn from others. Once we become aware and learn more about the topic, we can then have a seat at the table and join the conversation with our own claim. Read on for some ways to support students as they practice this foundational skill of working with claims!

🧭 Explore and Learn

As you know, one way to introduce students to multiple perspectives is by engaging with short excerpts. After practicing with excerpts, students are ready to study a pair or trio of full-length texts (including videos, infographics, and articles) on the same topic.

Through a Routine Argument Writing approach called “layering,” students read through a set of texts and add to their thinking and writing after each new text. As they learn more about a topic and research varying perspectives, their opinions often shift and evolve. This concept invites students to consider multiple perspectives before they make their own claim, and prepares them to manage more than one source in their written arguments.

Read through the overview document below and learn more about the layering approach to writing arguments. Click here to make your own template.

Next, we invite you to explore the lesson sequence in the collection below. This short unit uses the layering process to guide students as they consider varying perspectives found in longer texts. Students read and write their way through four different layered activities centered on the topic of Screen Time. Texts could be easily changed by topic or reading level.

Layering Reading, Writing, and Thinking Lesson Sequence

This lesson sequence uses the layering process to guide students as they move beyond short excerpts and consider varying perspectives found in longer ...

Screen Time Lesson Sequence.pdf

Layer #1: Becoming Aware

Layer 2: Expanding the Conversation

How Much Screen Time Is OK for My Kids? | Common Sense Media

How Much Screen Time Is OK for My Kids? - Learn more and get Common Sense Media's research-backed tips.

www.commonsensemedia.org

Layer 3: Add Another Text

AAP: Finding Ways to Keep Children Occupied During These Challenging Times

Families are doing their part to help contain the spread of the novel coronavirus by keeping children at home, which means finding creative ways to keep everyone calm, healthy and engaged in constructive work and play.

www.aap.org

Layer 4: Add a Final Text

How Much Screentime Is Too Much For Kids?

The key to "good" screen time is choosing wisely, not sweating the time your kids spend on the iPad.

www.romper.com

💬 Join the Discussion

Give it a try! Work through the Screen Time lesson sequence as a learner.

Once you are finished, join the discussion and reflect on your experience:

How did layering in multiple perspectives impact your thinking as you worked through the lesson?

How might your students respond to the layering approach? What might work well for them? What might be challenging?

Be sure to respond to posts of others!

🔦 Skill Spotlight: Writing and Revising Claims

The foundation of any argument is the writer’s claim. This specific and arguable statement, sometimes called the controlling idea or thesis, helps the reader understand the direction of the writer’s thinking. Students sometimes struggle to arrive at a claim about an issue and often confuse claims with facts or evidence.

Providing students with examples and non-examples of claims is one way for them to explore the difference: a claim is debatable (meaning others may disagree with it) and a claim is defensible (meaning that it can be defended with facts and evidence). Once students are comfortable with the process of reading sources and forming their own claim, they can revise and refine their claim to make sure it is compelling, debatable, and defensible.

Check out this slideshow with further information and considerations for working with claims:

Claim first or information first?

You probably noticed that this course did not begin with a focus on writing claims. ​In his book Teaching Argument Writing, George Hillocks asserts that a written argument should not begin with the writing of a claim:

Add caption for image (optional)

Although many teachers begin to teach some version of argument with the writing of a thesis statement (a claim), in reality, good argument begins with looking at the data that is likely to become the evidence in an argument and which gives rise to a thesis statement or major claim (xxi)

The most compelling claims and arguments grow from an exploration and understanding of the multiple perspectives surrounding a topic. Many times, our own thinking will shift as we research and discover new information. We can encourage students to delay making a claim until they have explored an issue more deeply.

💭Engage with your Thinking Partner!

Choose one of the claims you have made in the process of working through this course. Is it compelling? Is it debatable and defensible? If so, how do you know?

Try revising it using one of the sentence templates from the above slideshow.

Use the micro credential below to engage with your thinking partner!

Skill Spotlight: Writing and Revising Claims

Micro Credential

Crafting and Refining Argumentative Claims

This micro-credential recognizes your ability to guide students in crafting compelling, defensible claims that drive strong arguments. Effective argument writing is not just about stating an opinion—it’s about listening to multiple perspectives, analyzing evidence, and constructing well-reasoned claims. This credential demonstrates your expertise in teaching students to refine their claims based on layered learning, consider opposing viewpoints, and build arguments that contribute meaningfully to academic discussions.
